Key Characteristics & Etiology: Most common CHD overall (25-30%); Defect in membranous or muscular interventricular septum
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Left-to-Right shunt resulting in pulmonary hyperperfusion, volume overload of LA and LV, and eventual pulmonary hypertension
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Pansystolic murmur at lower left sternal border, thrill, tachypnea, poor feeding, failure to thrive; Red Flags: Heart failure, Eisenmenger syndrome
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Echocardiogram (gold standard), CXR cardiomegaly; Diuretics (Furosemide) + ACE inhibitors (Captopril) + Surgical repair

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Failure of ductus arteriosus closure post-birth; High incidence in preterm infants and congenital rubella
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Persistent L-to-R shunting from aorta to pulmonary artery causing pulmonary overcirculation and wide pulse pressure
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Continuous 'machinery' murmur at left infraclavicular area, bounding peripheral pulses, wide pulse pressure; Red Flags: Heart failure, pulmonary hypertension
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Echocardiogram; Indomethacin/IV Ibuprofen for ductal closure in preterms; Surgical ligation or device closure if persistent

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Most common cyanotic CHD beyond infant period; Anterosuperior deviation of infundibular septum
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: 4 features: (1) Large VSD, (2) RVOTO/Infundibular stenosis, (3) Overriding aorta, (4) RV hypertrophy; Right-to-Left shunt causes cyanosis
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Central cyanosis, clubbing, single S2, ejection systolic murmur; Red Flags: Hypercyanotic 'Tet' spells (hyperpnea, deep cyanosis, syncope)
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: CXR: 'Boot-shaped' heart (coeur en sabot), Echocardiogram; Tet Spell Rx: Knee-chest position + 100% O2 + Morphine; Complete surgical repair

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Discrete narrowing of aortic lumen near insertion of ductus arteriosus; Associated with Turner Syndrome (45,X)
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Mechanical obstruction to LV outflow causing upper limb hypertension and lower extremity hypoperfusion
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Upper extremity hypertension, weak/delayed femoral pulses, radio-femoral delay, cold lower limbs; Red Flags: Severe heart failure, intracranial hemorrhage
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Echocardiogram, CT/MR angiography, rib notching on CXR; PGE1 infusion in duct-dependent neonates; Surgical repair or balloon angioplasty

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Aorta arises from RV and pulmonary artery arises from LV; Most common cyanotic CHD in newborns
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Parallel circulations incompatible with life unless mixing exists via VSD, ASD, or PDA
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Profound cyanosis within first hours of life unresponsive to 100% oxygen, tachypnea, single S2; Red Flags: Severe metabolic acidosis, hypoxemia
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: CXR: 'Egg-on-a-string' cardiac contour with narrow mediastinum, Echocardiogram; Immediate PGE1 infusion + Balloon Atrial Septostomy + Arterial Switch Surgery

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Autoimmune non-suppurative reaction 2-4 weeks post-Group A Streptococcal pharyngitis
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Molecular mimicry between GAS M-protein and human cardiac myosin/valvular tissues causing pancarditis
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Major Jones criteria: Carditis (MR murmur), Migratory polyarthritis, Sydenham chorea, Erythema marginatum, Subcutaneous nodules
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Elevated ASO titer / Anti-DNase B, high ESR/CRP, ECG PR prolongation, Echocardiogram; IM Benzathine Penicillin G + High-dose Aspirin/Prednisolone

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Acute self-limiting medium-vessel necrotizing vasculitis peaking in children <5 years
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Immune-mediated endothelial inflammation with high predilection for coronary artery infiltration and aneurysm formation
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Fever >=5 days + 4/5 criteria: conjunctivitis, mucositis (strawberry tongue), polymorphic rash, extremity changes, cervical lymphadenopathy; Red Flags: Coronary aneurysms
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: High ESR/CRP, thrombocytosis, Echocardiogram (coronary dilation); Single-dose IVIG (2 g/kg) + High-dose Aspirin within 10 days

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Most common pediatric symptomatic arrhythmia; AV nodal re-entrant tachycardia (AVNRT) or accessory pathway (WPW)
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Rapid paroxysmal re-entrant circuit resulting in ventricular heart rate >220 bpm in infants or >180 bpm in children
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Palpitations, tachypnea, poor feeding, pallor, rapid regular pulse; Red Flags: Decompensated shock, lethargy, pulmonary edema
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: ECG: Narrow QRS tachycardia with absent or abnormal P waves; Stable Rx: Vagal maneuvers (ice to face) -> Rapid IV Adenosine bolus; Unstable Rx: Synchronized DC Cardioversion (0.5-1 J/kg)

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Bacterial (S. viridans, S. aureus) or fungal infection of endocardium; Pre-existing CHD is major risk factor
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Endothelial damage creates non-bacterial thrombotic endocarditis where circulating bacteria adhere, forming vegetations
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Fever, new or changing cardiac murmur, splenomegaly, petechiae; Red Flags: Embolic strokes, Roth spots, Janeway lesions, Osler nodes
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Duke Criteria: Serial blood cultures positive + Echocardiogram showing vegetation/abscess; High-dose IV Antibiotics for 4-6 weeks + Surgical repair if valvular destruction

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Inability of heart to meet metabolic demands; Caused by volume overload (VSD, PDA), pressure overload (Coarctation), or myocardial dysfunction
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Neurohormonal activation (RAAS and SNS) causing sodium/water retention, cardiomegaly, and pulmonary/systemic venous congestion
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Tachypnea, diaphoresis during feeds, failure to thrive, hepatomegaly, cardiomegaly, gallop rhythm; Red Flags: Cardiogenic shock, severe pulmonary edema
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: CXR cardiomegaly and pulmonary edema, Echocardiogram, elevated BNP; Loop Diuretics (Furosemide) + ACE Inhibitors (Captopril) + Spironolactone
